questions.stem: Choose the word that is closest in meaning to CANDID.
questions.explanation: 'Candid' means open and truthful in what one says; 'frank' carries the same sense of speaking honestly.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to GENEROUS.
questions.explanation: 'Generous' means willing to give freely; its opposite is 'stingy'. 'Giving' is a synonym placed as a trap.

questions.stem: Which word means 'speaking or done in few words; using very little speech'?
questions.explanation: 'Terse' describes speech that is brief and to the point, sometimes abruptly so. The other options all begin with 't' but carry unrelated meanings.

questions.stem: Which single word can mean BOTH 'a small stick with a tip that bursts into flame when struck' AND 'a game or contest between two teams'?
questions.explanation: 'Match' means a fire-stick (from Old French) and, quite separately, a contest (from Old English) -- same spelling and sound, different origins.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'a wild goose chase' mean?

options.text: A hopeless search or pursuit that leads nowhere
A warning of danger to come
An argument that quickly turns angry
A piece of very good luck

questions.explanation: A 'wild goose chase' is a pointless pursuit of something that cannot be caught or found, so all the effort is wasted.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is closest in meaning to FLEETING.
questions.explanation: 'Fleeting' describes something that lasts only a very short time; 'momentary' shares that meaning.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The path grew increasingly OBSCURE as night fell', which word means the opposite of the capitalised word?
questions.explanation: 'Obscure' here means hard to see or make out; its opposite is 'clear'. 'Hidden' is a synonym of 'obscure', set to catch the careless.

questions.stem: Which word describes easing pain or making a hardship less severe?
questions.explanation: To 'alleviate' pain is to ease it. 'Aggravate', which means to make worse, is the tempting near-opposite; the rest are unrelated 'a' words.

questions.stem: Which single word can mean BOTH 'the sound a dog makes' AND 'the outer covering of a tree trunk'?
questions.explanation: 'Bark' is the noise a dog makes and, separately, the skin of a tree; the two senses arrived in English from unrelated words.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to bury the hatchet' mean?

options.text: To frighten someone with a sudden loud noise
To make peace and end a quarrel
To borrow money and not pay it back
To spoil a celebration by arriving late

questions.explanation: To 'bury the hatchet' is to settle a dispute and become friendly again, from the custom of burying weapons to mark peace.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The detective was METICULOUS in checking every clue', which word could best replace the capitalised word without changing the meaning?
questions.explanation: 'Meticulous' means showing great care over every small detail; a 'thorough' search checks everything, matching the sense. 'Suspicious' describes the detective's attitude, not his carefulness.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to FEEBLE.
questions.explanation: 'Feeble' means weak; its opposite is 'sturdy'. 'Frail' is a synonym of 'feeble' offered as a trap.

questions.stem: What does the word TRANSPARENT mean?

options.text: Allowing light to pass through so objects behind can be seen
Producing a bright light of its own
Having a smooth and highly polished surface
Changing colour when it is heated
Reflecting almost all the light that falls on it

questions.explanation: 'Transparent' means see-through: light passes through it. A shiny or reflective surface is a common confusion, but that is not the same as being see-through.

questions.stem: Which single word can mean BOTH 'treating everyone equally and justly' AND 'a large outdoor event with rides and stalls'?
questions.explanation: 'Fair' can describe just treatment and can also name a funfair; the two words share their spelling by accident of history, not meaning.

questions.stem: Complete the idiom: 'They handed in the project at the ______ hour, only minutes before the deadline.'
questions.explanation: The set phrase is 'at the eleventh hour', meaning at the very last possible moment. The other words fit the sentence loosely but are not the fixed idiom.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is closest in meaning to ABUNDANT.
questions.explanation: 'Abundant' means existing in large quantities; 'plentiful' has the same meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to ANCIENT.
questions.explanation: 'Ancient' means very old; its opposite is 'modern'. 'Aged' is a synonym set as a trap.

questions.stem: What does the word VACANT mean?
questions.explanation: 'Vacant' means empty or unoccupied, as in a vacant seat. 'Crowded' is the opposite, offered to catch a guess.

questions.stem: Which single word can mean BOTH 'a long, slender rod of wood or metal' AND 'either of the two points at the far ends of the Earth's axis'?
questions.explanation: 'Pole' meaning a rod (from Latin 'palus') and 'pole' meaning the end of an axis (from Latin 'polus') are two different words that look and sound the same.

questions.stem: Complete the idiom: 'He tidies his room only once in a ______ moon.'
questions.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely. 'Full moon' and 'harvest moon' are real terms but not this idiom.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'Her reluctant apology satisfied no one', which word is nearest in meaning to the capitalised word?
questions.explanation: 'Reluctant' means doing something without wanting to; 'unwilling' captures that hesitation. 'Sincere' is nearly its opposite, which is why it tempts.

questions.stem: Choose the word that is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to PERMIT.
questions.explanation: To 'permit' is to let something happen; its opposite is to 'forbid'. 'Allow' is a synonym placed as a trap.

questions.stem: What does the word NOVICE mean?

options.text: A person who teaches a difficult skill
A person who competes for a prize
A person who travels from place to place
A person who is new to and inexperienced at an activity
A person who refuses to obey the rules

questions.explanation: A 'novice' is a beginner, new to an activity. An expert or teacher is the opposite idea, set as a distractor.

questions.stem: Which single word can mean BOTH 'a unit of money used in Britain' AND 'to hit something hard, over and over'?
questions.explanation: 'Pound' the money (from Latin 'pondo') and 'pound' meaning to beat (from Old English 'punian') have different origins but the same spelling and sound.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to beat around the bush' mean?

options.text: To search everywhere for something lost
To avoid coming to the main point
To work extremely hard at a task
To make a situation far worse

questions.explanation: To 'beat around the bush' is to talk around a subject instead of saying plainly what one means.
